messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 25
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Counselor
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 48

At 25, she is already someone other people turn to when they are falling apart. She works as a counselor at a community nonprofit, spending her days listening carefully, reflecting feelings back, helping clients name what has happened to them. Before the incident, she takes pride in being steady. She is the daughter of South Asian immigrants, raised to be composed, respectful, and hardworking. She lives alone now, not far from her office, and imagines herself building a life around service, independence, and a quiet kind of competence.

The night that keeps returning begins as an ordinary one. She is driving home after meeting a friend for dinner. She is tired but relaxed, replaying bits of conversation in her head, when she notices flashing lights behind her. She pulls over quickly, assuming it is a routine stop. At first she is more embarrassed than afraid. She checks her mirrors, reaches for her license, and tries to remember all the rules about keeping her hands visible. When the officer approaches, his voice is already sharp. She feels herself become extra polite, her words careful and softened. She answers his questions, but the exchange turns confusing almost immediately. He says she is not moving fast enough. She tries to explain what she is reaching for. He tells her to get out of the car.

What she remembers most clearly is the speed with which the moment changes. One second she is trying to comply; the next she is being yanked forward. Her cheek hits the side of the car. There is a burst of pain in her shoulder, then the pressure of hands forcing her down. She hears herself saying, “I’m listening, I’m listening,” in a voice that sounds young and strange to her. People are watching from somewhere she cannot see. She becomes intensely aware of her body as an object being handled. She thinks, with a kind of cold disbelief, that if she makes one wrong move she could die. Later she will remember the asphalt against her skin, the weight on her back, and the officer’s command to stop resisting when she is not resisting at all.

She is released without charges after hours that feel unreal. By then, the adrenaline has drained away, leaving her shaky and nauseated. She calls her older sister from the parking lot and cannot form a coherent sentence. In the days that follow, she tells the story in fragments: to family, to a supervisor when she cannot come in, to a friend who urges her to file a complaint. Each retelling makes her chest tighten. At night she lies awake waiting for sleep and then dreads it when it comes. She jerks awake from dreams in which she cannot breathe, her heart pounding so hard she has to turn on all the lights. Sometimes she sees the patrol lights flashing across her bedroom ceiling even when the room is dark and still.

When she returns to work, she finds that the things she usually offers others are suddenly difficult to access for herself. She sits across from clients and remains outwardly attentive, but part of her is scanning constantly: footsteps in the hallway, a raised male voice in the lobby, the crackle of a police radio from the street below. If a client talks about authority figures, her stomach drops. During one session, a teenager describes being shoved during a school search, and she feels heat rush through her body so quickly she loses track of what the girl is saying. She recovers professionally, but afterward locks herself in the office bathroom and cries in angry, silent bursts.

She begins reorganizing her life around not feeling caught off guard. She changes her route home to avoid the street where she was stopped. If she sees a police car in traffic, she grips the steering wheel until her hands ache and will sometimes pull into a parking lot to let it pass. She stops going out in the evening unless absolutely necessary. Friends notice she declines invitations with excuses that sound reasonable but repeated. Her world grows smaller in ways she tells herself are practical.

She is troubled by how much the experience has altered her sense of herself. She used to feel confident in her ability to de-escalate tense situations, to read people, to stay grounded. Now she second-guesses her own memory—whether her hand moved too quickly, whether her tone changed, whether she somehow caused what happened. Another part of her is furious at that line of thinking and ashamed that it has lodged inside her at all. She feels especially alone when older relatives urge her to “let it go” and be careful not to make trouble. Their fear is familiar; so is the message beneath it.

Months later, she still lives with the stop as if it has not fully ended. Sirens make her shoulders tense before she knows why. She startles when someone approaches her car window. She keeps replaying the officer’s face and the feeling of helplessness under his hands. At work she remains deeply compassionate with clients, but she notices how exhausted she is by the effort of appearing calm. Some mornings she sits in her parked car outside the office, breathing through the urge to turn around and go home, then walks in anyway, carrying both her training and her fear together.
